issues.legal_issue: A second review of the same judgment is not maintainable when the first review has been dismissed and the later application presents no qualifying new evidence or apparent error.
material_facts: The respondents had already sought review of the judgment and their first review applications were dismissed after the grounds raised had been considered.

In the second review applications, the respondents filed certified copies of revenue records, although they had previously filed photocopies of the same records and had several earlier opportunities to produce certified copies.

The respondents did not explain that the documents were unknown to them or could not have been obtained despite due diligence before the judgment, and they identified no error apparent on the face of the record.

The earlier order of the Supreme Court left open the possibility of approaching the High Court with documents said to show surrender, but the documents later produced were not new and had been available earlier.
issues.conclusion: The second review applications were not maintainable and amounted to an abuse of the process of the court. The appeals were allowed, the order allowing the second reviews was set aside, and the earlier judgment was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 114 and Order XLVII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure permit review only on discovery of new and important matter or evidence that, despite due diligence, was not previously known or could not be produced, an error apparent on the face of the record, or another sufficient reason analogous to those grounds. Review is not an appeal in disguise, does not permit reappreciation of evidence or repetition of rejected arguments, and a dismissed review cannot be followed by another review of the same judgment. The Court relied on Lily Thomas v. Union of India, which states that no further review lies after dismissal of a review; Kamlesh Verma v. Mayawati, which summarizes grounds on which review is and is not maintainable; Parsion Devi v. Sumitri Devi and Thungabhadra Industries Ltd. v. Government of A.P., on the distinction between an apparent error and an erroneous decision; State of West Bengal v. Kamal Sengupta, on the need to show that new evidence was previously unavailable despite due diligence and could have affected the judgment; and Aribam Tuleshwar Sharma v. Aribam Pishak Sharma, on the limits of review jurisdiction. The Court also relied on the principles in Col. Avatar Singh Sekhon, Kerala State Electricity Board v. Hitech Electrothermics, Jain Studios, and Chajju Ram v. Neki Ram, among other cited cases.

rule.if: second_review_proceeding and first_review_dismissed and documents_previously_available and no_due_diligence_explanation and no_apparent_error_identified

predicates.second_review_proceeding: A party filed a further application seeking review of the same judgment after an earlier review application concerning that judgment.
predicates.first_review_dismissed: The court had dismissed the party's earlier application to review that judgment.
predicates.documents_previously_available: The party relied on documents that it had already possessed, submitted in earlier proceedings, or had earlier opportunities to obtain.
predicates.no_due_diligence_explanation: The party did not explain that the documents were unknown or could not have been obtained earlier despite reasonable diligence.
predicates.no_apparent_error_identified: The party did not identify a patent error evident from the record that required correction.
predicates.second_review_not_maintainable: The further application to review the judgment cannot be entertained.

issues.definition: When a party seeks review again after an earlier review was dismissed, relies on documents available earlier without explaining why they could not have been obtained, and identifies no apparent error, the further review cannot be entertained.
